questions.question: A chemist drops an antacid tablet into a beaker of cool water, and it fizzes hard. On the bench beside it, a second beaker of water boils over a burner, bubbling just as hard. Which bubbles are made of a new substance?
questions.answer: Only the bubbles from the tablet
choices: Only the bubbles from the tablet
Only the bubbles in the boiling water
The bubbles in both of the beakers
The bubbles in neither of the beakers
questions.context: Once the tablet is wet, two of its ingredients react and make carbon dioxide, a gas that was not there before, so bubbles rising from a liquid that is not boiling are a clue to a new substance. The bubbles in boiling water are only water turned into a gas, a change of state that makes nothing new, which is why bubbles alone are a clue and not proof.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.6E has 6th graders use a gas given off as evidence of a possible chemical change, and boiling water is the standard case of bubbles with no new substance.

questions.question: A skier tears open the airtight wrapper of a hand warmer, a cloth pouch of iron powder mixed with salt and a little water, and shakes it. Within minutes the pouch is hot, though it holds no flame and no battery. What makes the heat?
choices: The iron rusting very fast
The iron grains rubbing together
The salt dissolving in the water
Sunlight soaked up by the iron
questions.context: With the wrapper open, oxygen from the air reaches the damp iron and it rusts, a chemical change that gives off heat, and the salt speeds it up. An iron gate rusts too, but so slowly that its heat spreads away unfelt; the fine powder rusts fast enough to stay hot for hours. Dissolving salt gives off no heat at all.
questions.grade_note: A change in temperature on its own is one of the signs of a chemical change that TEKS 6.6E names, and an iron hand warmer is a common classroom example of a reaction that gets hot.

questions.question: A student blows gently through a straw into a test tube of clear limewater. Within a minute the liquid has turned cloudy and milky white. What makes it milky?
questions.answer: Tiny grains of a solid formed in it
choices: Tiny grains of a solid formed in it
Tiny bubbles of her breath caught in it
Tiny drops of mist from her warm breath
Tiny specks of dust she blew into it
questions.context: Carbon dioxide in her breath reacts with the lime dissolved in the water and makes calcium carbonate, the stuff of chalk and limestone, which does not dissolve. Its tiny white grains hang in the liquid: a solid that appears in a liquid this way is called a precipitate, and it is a clue to a new substance. Bubbles of breath rise and burst, leaving the water clear.
questions.grade_note: A precipitate, a solid forming in a liquid, is one of the signs of chemical change named in TEKS 6.6E, and breath turning limewater milky is a classic classroom test.

questions.question: A new copper roof gleams reddish-orange in the sun. Over the years of rain and wind that follow, it slowly turns a pale blue-green all over. What turns it green?
questions.answer: The copper reacting with air and rain
choices: The copper reacting with air and rain
Moss and algae growing over the copper
Rain washing the shine off the copper
Sunlight fading the copper's colour
questions.context: Copper slowly reacts with oxygen, carbon dioxide and water from the air and the rain, and builds a green crust called a patina, a new substance with a new colour. The patina clings tight and shields the copper beneath it, which is one reason a copper roof can last more than a hundred years.
questions.grade_note: A colour change is one of the signs of a chemical change 6th graders learn, and a copper roof turning green is a standard example of it.

questions.question: A camper bends a plastic glow stick until something inside it snaps with a crack, then shakes it. The stick glows bright green for hours, though it holds no battery. Where does its light come from?
questions.answer: Two liquids reacting as they mix
choices: Two liquids reacting as they mix
Daylight it soaked up and stored
Heat from the snapping inside it
Sparks of static from the shaking
questions.context: Bending the stick breaks a thin glass vial, and shaking mixes the liquid inside the vial with the liquid around it. The two react and give off light with very little heat, so the light is a clue to a chemical change. Glow-in-the-dark toys work another way: they soak up light and give it back slowly, but a glow stick needs no light first.
questions.grade_note: Light given off is among the signs of a chemical change taught in 6th grade, and the glow stick is the everyday example of a reaction that makes light.

questions.question: A runner's fresh sweat has almost no smell. By the end of a long, hot race, though, the armpits of her shirt smell strongly. What makes the smell?
choices: Bacteria breaking the sweat down
Sweat drying until its smell is strong
Salt that the drying sweat leaves
Sweat soaking deep into the cloth
questions.context: Bacteria that live on the skin feed on sweat and turn some of it into new, smelly substances, so a new smell is a clue that a chemical change has happened. Fresh sweat is mostly water with a little salt and fat, and drying it or soaking it into cloth makes nothing new, so neither can give it a smell it never had.
questions.grade_note: A new smell is one of the clues to a chemical change that 6th graders learn, and body odour is an everyday body example of it.

questions.question: A geologist rubs a shiny, steel-grey lump of the mineral hematite across a rough white tile. It leaves a reddish-brown streak of fine powder behind. What is the reddish-brown powder?
questions.answer: The same mineral, ground very fine
choices: The same mineral, ground very fine
A new substance made by the rubbing
Powder from the tile, stained red
A different red rock inside the lump
questions.context: Rubbing only grinds the hematite into tiny grains, a physical change that makes no new substance, yet the powder of many minerals is a different colour from the lump. Geologists call that colour the streak and use it to tell minerals apart. So a colour change by itself is a clue to a new substance, never proof.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that crushing or grinding is a physical change and that a colour change is evidence, not proof; the streak test is the rock-lab case of both.

questions.question: A burning log and a lit match both give off heat. In a lab, a teacher stirs two white powders together in a flask, and it turns so cold that the wet wooden block it stands on freezes fast to the glass. Can a change that turns cold on its own be a chemical change?
questions.answer: Yes, some reactions take in heat
choices: Yes, some reactions take in heat
Yes, some reactions give off cold
No, reactions only ever give off heat
No, only melting can make things colder
questions.context: The two powders, barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride, react and make ammonia gas, water and a new solid, and the reaction draws in heat from everything around it, so the flask drops to about 20 degrees Celsius below zero. Cold is not a thing that flows out of the powders; the flask feels cold because heat leaves whatever touches it. A change in temperature either way can be a clue to a chemical change.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.6E names a change in thermal energy as evidence of a chemical change, and 6th graders learn that a reaction can get colder as well as hotter.
